query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated degradation in eutectic high-entropy alloys under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures is driven by a dual mechanism: mechanical wear disrupts the protective, friction‐induced oxide film while the exposed, compositionally heterogeneous phase boundaries (with differing electrochemical potentials) promote galvanic coupling and localized pitting. This feedback loop intensifies both material removal and oxide spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a fine lamellar microstructure comprising alternating FCC and BCC (or B2) phases and an initially intact, friction-induced oxide film.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosive attack (e.g., chloride-containing environment) at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature under atmospherical or corrosive conditions that promote both oxidation and active wear; simultaneous mechanical sliding (friction) and exposure to corrosive species.
generation.structural_mediator: The mechanically formed protective oxide film and the microstructural phase boundaries between the eutectic FCC and BCC phases that possess different electrochemical activities.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating and mechanical shear under sliding conditions form an initial protective oxide layer; however, repeated stress causes micro-cracking and spallation of this layer. Once disrupted, the exposed phase boundaries—with inherent compositional and potential differences—act as sites for galvanic coupling. This galvanic effect accelerates localized pitting corrosion, which further undermines the surface integrity, thereby enhancing the wear rate in a synergistic feedback loop.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous wear and corrosive attack, total degradation (material loss) will be significantly higher than under wear-only or corrosion-only conditions. Both the depth of wear tracks and the density/size of corrosion pits will increase relative to a baseline sample. The oxide layer will be found to be more fragmented and less protective, especially near the phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: The same alloy exposed to either isolated wear (in an inert or non-corrosive atmosphere) or isolated corrosion (without mechanical sliding) under similar elevated temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures under high-temperature conditions (approx. 600–900 °C) in environments where mechanical friction and aggressive corrosive species (e.g., chlorides) are simultaneously present.
generation.uncertainty: The precise relative contributions of mechanical oxide spallation versus galvanic-driven pitting corrosion, as well as the quantitative increase in degradation rates, remain uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and testing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical specimens of the eutectic HEA and subject one group to simultaneous high-temperature sliding wear in a chloride-containing solution, while two control groups are exposed separately: one group to sliding wear in an inert atmosphere and the other to static immersion in the corrosive solution at the same temperature. Use identical test durations and environmental parameters.
measurements: Quantitative measurement of wear track depth using laser scanning microscopy
Evaluation of corrosion pit density and size via SEM with EDS analysis
XRD or XPS characterization of oxide film integrity and composition
Electrochemical impedance and polarization tests to assess passivation quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear-corrosion group does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in total degradation (with markers such as deeper wear tracks, more extensive pit formation, and more fragmented oxide films) compared to the additive effects observed in the isolated wear and isolated corrosion groups, then the hypothesis that the synergistic mechanisms (oxide disruption coupled with galvanic pitting) are responsible for accelerated degradation will be falsified.

Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.
